 Mark Kiszla: Most overpaid coach in the USA earns his keep in CU win
 By Mark Kiszla 
 Published October 31, 2026 8:16pm 
 + 
 Add Denver Gazette on Google
 Colorado Buffaloes head coach Deion Sanders, right, cheers as Colorado Buffaloes running back Richard Young (9) heads back onto the field after scoring the first touchdown of the game during the first half of the CU vs Kansas State Football game at Folsom Field on Saturday, Oct. 31, 2026.
(Stephen Swofford, Denver Gazette) 
 ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT 
 BOULDER – For once, the Buffaloes of Deion Sanders didn’t blow it. And the biggest sigh of relief in Folsom Field was heard from the man who gave Coach Prime at least $25 million more than he’s worth.
 “About time!” Rick George exclaimed Saturday as he bounded down a stairwell of the Champions Center on the CU campus.

 Just when it looked as if the Buffs might not ever win again, they tried mightily to lose against Kansas State, but escaped with a 27-24 victory in overtime.
 “It should’ve never got to overtime,” said Sanders, aware there are losing habits still to be eradicated. “We allowed some crazy things to happen. But in all, we got the victory.”
 ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT 
 After tight end Charlie Williams caught an 11-yard touchdown pass from Isaac Wilson in the opening round of overtime to end the agony of more than a month of defeats, CU students dressed as Chester Cheetah, rainbow unicorns and every character in the “Star Wars” universe stormed the field.
 And doesn’t that crazy Halloween picture say more than 1,000 words about the sorry current state of the CU football program?
 When ending a five-game losing streak is reason enough for the fanbase to stage a happy riot, you know how desperate Buffaloes were to bury their misery.
 Maybe none of the 46,325 witnesses in the stadium was more desperate than George, the CU athletic director emeritus who gave Sanders a five-year, $54 million contract extension as one of his last big acts on the job.
 ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT 
 This CU football season has been a painful exercise in buyer’s remorse.
 With their television ratings plummeting and sellouts at home no longer guaranteed, the Buffs had fallen to the bottom of the Big 12 Conference standings and it was beginning to look as if they might never get up. 
 Although Colorado deserves praise for smashing K-State in the mouth with 240 yards rushing and Wilson emerged victorious for the first time as the team’s starting quarterback, this game was decided during a tense and odd sequence during the edgy final seconds of the fourth quarter.
 How to describe what happened?
 ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT 
 Well, there’s no delicate way to put it.
 Given a chance to bury Coach Prime, two proud sons of Colorado representing the visiting Wildcats inexplicably turned into scaredy cats.
 Kansas State quarterback Blake Barnett, who guided nearby Erie High School to a state championship while breaking legendary Christian McCaffrey’s record for most touchdowns produced in a prep career, had led the Wildcats on a mad dash down the field during the final minute of the fourth quarter.
 His 8-yard touchdown pass to tight end Garret Oakley a mere two seconds prior to the final gun pulled the Wildcats within a single point, down 21-20.
 ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT 
 With Folsom Field in a here-we-go-again panic and CU’s defense reeling in retreat, everybody in the joint was certain what the Wildcats would do.
 They would go for two, and dare Colorado to fold. Again.
 Kansas State had the dagger raised. Barnett and his offensive teammates huddled on the field, fully prepared to run a play for a two-point conversion that would decide the outcome in dramatic, win-or-go-home fashion.
 And then?
 For some inexplicable reason, after Colorado took a timeout to restore the equilibrium in spinning heads of young Buffs standing with their backs to the end zone, Kansas State coach Collin Klein lost his nerve and reneged on his trust in Barnett and the Wildcats.
 “I was ready to go make a play to win the game,” Buffaloes linebacker Gideon “ESPN” Lampron said.
 So give these Buffs their due. Bruised repeatedly by adversity and quarterback controversy as this season swirled down the tubes, a CU team with every reason to blink refused to back down in the face of a challenge.
 “I’m happy,” Sanders told me, “because they showed enough fight that the opposition ended up not going for two. (The Wildcats) said: ‘Ut-oh. No, no, no.’ ”
 Klein, who grew up as a football hero at Loveland High School, said after looking at CU’s defensive adjustments during the timeout, he eschewed the chance for sudden victory because “I didn’t feel as good about it.”
 Those who hesitate are lost. And K-State now joins the Buffs in last place in the Big 12 with a 1-4 record in conference play.
 Barnett, whose stellar high school career unfolded less than 20 miles down the road from the CU campus, got his first real playing time in an injury-plagued season after entering the game late in the first quarter. He passed for 224 yards and ran for 40 more against the Buffs.
 “He hasn’t practiced a whole lot, so to have that type of gutsy performance and play the way he did to give us chances down the field like he did with three touchdown passes, I’m incredibly proud of him,” Klein said. “And I’m just tore up that we couldn’t get over the hump for him.”
 At 3-5 overall, it would take a minor football miracle for Colorado to become bowl eligible. But I’m saying there’s a chance, even if on the surface of it, it might sound dumber than dumb to anyone who has watched the Buffs play or followed criticism on the internet.
 “We don’t subscribe to your channels.” Sanders said, still defiant despite the “We Comin'” days being a distant and fading memory.
